passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Dog-Free Zone in the Park

emails.subject: Proposed dog restriction, Larchfield Common — consultation response
emails.body:
Dear Parks Department,

I am responding to the consultation on restricting dogs from the eastern meadow at Larchfield Common. I own a dog and I support the proposal, which I mention because I suspect most responses will sort neatly into owners against and non-owners for.

The eastern meadow is where the ground-nesting birds are, and a dog off a lead there is a problem regardless of how well behaved it is — the birds do not distinguish. That is a fact about birds, not a judgement about owners, and I wish the consultation document had put it that way, because as written it reads as though owners are being blamed.

My objection is to the map. The proposed boundary runs along the path that is the only accessible route from the Elm Street gate to the rest of the Common. Restricting dogs from the meadow is reasonable; restricting them from that path means anyone who arrives at the Elm Street gate with a dog cannot get anywhere. I do not think that was intended, and I do not think anyone with a dog walked the boundary before it was drawn.

Moving the line twenty metres north puts the path outside the restriction and takes nothing away from the birds.

Sincerely,
Nkechi Obiorah

emails.subject: RE: Proposed dog restriction, Larchfield Common — consultation response
emails.body:
Dear Ms Obiorah,

Nobody with a dog walked the boundary. You are right, and it is the sort of thing that is obvious once written down and invisible until someone does.

The line was drawn from the ecological survey, which mapped the nesting area accurately, and then transferred to the plan without anyone checking what it did to circulation. Our ecologist was not asked about access and would not have been the right person to ask.

On the substance: your twenty-metre suggestion works. The nesting area does not extend to the path, and the ecologist has confirmed the margin is sufficient. The revised map goes to committee on 6 May and I have credited your response in the report, since the change came from it.

On your point about the wording, I want to be careful not to over-promise. I agree the document reads as blame and I have asked for it to be rewritten around the birds rather than around behaviour. I do not control the final wording — that sits with communications — so I can tell you I have asked and not that it will change.

One thing I should add rather than let you discover it. The restriction as revised still removes the only unfenced off-lead area on the north side of the town. That is a genuine loss to owners and it is not offset anywhere in the current plan. I have raised it separately as a gap, but it would carry more weight from residents than from me.

Regards,
Dominic Fairbairn
Parks Development Officer

passages.title: What Cities Get Wrong About Dogs
passages.content:
Urban dog policy is usually written as a conflict between owners and everyone else, and the resulting rules tend to satisfy neither group. Research on how shared space is actually used suggests the framing itself is the problem, and that several of the assumptions built into standard policy do not survive contact with evidence.

The first assumption is that off-lead access is a convenience. For most dogs it is closer to a requirement: sustained off-lead running is difficult to substitute, and dogs deprived of it show the behaviours — pulling, reactivity, excessive barking — that generate the complaints prompting further restriction. Policy that removes off-lead space without replacing it therefore tends to increase the problems it was written to reduce, on a delay long enough that the connection is rarely drawn.

The second concerns where conflict actually occurs. Complaints cluster overwhelmingly at boundaries and bottlenecks — gates, narrow paths, the strip where an off-lead area meets a playground — rather than across open space. This matters because the standard response is to shrink the permitted area, which increases the ratio of boundary to interior and concentrates encounters at precisely the points where they were already happening. Widening buffers and separating entrances performs better than reducing area, and costs less.

Enforcement evidence is uncomfortable for everyone. Fines for fouling are almost never issued relative to the scale of the problem, because the offence requires an officer to witness it. What measurably reduces fouling is bin provision and placement — the effect of a bin at a path junction is larger and cheaper than any enforcement campaign yet evaluated. Signage alone performs poorly, and signage listing penalties performs no better than signage that does not.

There is also a distributional pattern that rarely enters the debate. Restrictions concentrate in denser neighbourhoods where public space is scarcest, because that is where competing demands are highest. The households affected are disproportionately those without private gardens, who have no alternative. The result is that the owners least able to absorb a restriction absorb most of them.

None of this argues that shared space needs no rules. It argues that the effective ones are structural — where the entrances are, where the bins are, how wide the buffers are — and that the rules cities reach for first are the ones evidence supports least.

viewpoints.name: Councillor Estelle Marchetti
viewpoints.text: We run a licensing scheme and I will be plain that it does not do what people assume. It does not improve behaviour and there is no evidence it reduces incidents — responsible owners license and the others do not, which is the problem with every voluntary-in-practice scheme. What it does do is fund the bins, the wardens and the off-lead maintenance, and it does that reliably. I would defend it as a hypothecated charge for services owners use, and I would not defend it as a safety measure.

viewpoints.name: Farhan Qureshi, veterinarian
viewpoints.text: My concern is what licensing displaces in the public conversation. Registration tells you an animal exists; microchipping and up-to-date contact details tell you whose it is when it is found, and the second is what actually reunites lost animals and establishes responsibility after an incident. Many schemes collect a fee and never check the chip record is current, which is the part that matters. If a city wants one intervention, make chip-record accuracy the requirement and let the fee follow it.

viewpoints.name: Ivy Robinson-Clarke, dog owner
viewpoints.text: I license mine and I would still argue the cost falls in the wrong place. A flat fee is regressive — the same amount to a household that has a garden and a car and to one that walks to a shared park because it has neither. And it is the second household that already absorbs most of the restrictions. Scale the fee, waive it on low incomes, or accept that you are charging the people with the least access for the space they have least of.

viewpoints.name: Dr Marcus Ebele, public health researcher
viewpoints.text: Both sides cite bite statistics and both should stop. The data are collected from hospital presentations, so they capture severity rather than frequency, and they under-record incidents involving children and the household's own animal, which is where most bites occur. Whether licensing changes any of that is simply unknown — no scheme I am aware of has been evaluated against a comparable unlicensed area. I am not opposed. I am saying nobody currently has grounds to claim it works.
